Affiliation:: Advanced Radar Research Center (ARRC), The University of Oklahoma; NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL)
Techniques Used: Hybrid simulation (embedded element pattern x array factor)
Data & Platforms: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (JHU-APL)
Key Research Thinking Patterns: All-Digital Architecture for Adaptive Surveillance: Leveraging element-level control in fully digital phased arrays to enable rapid volume scanning and real-time adaptive beamforming, as demonstrated by the Horus S-band radar's capability to replace legacy WSR-88D systems with higher temporal resolution.

Hybrid Optimization for Multi-Beam Synthesis: Utilizing Bezier-surface parametrization and phase-only optimization frameworks to synthesize custom transmit beams with multiple simultaneous peaks, thereby enhancing temporal resolution and sidelobe isolation without significant sensitivity loss.

Precision Mutual Coupling Calibration: Implementing reference-based recursive far-field calibration and ground-truth error estimation using UAS platforms to align array elements with high precision (±0.15 dB), ensuring robust polarimetric accuracy for hydrometeor classification.

Reduced-Aperture Performance Validation: Evaluating radar performance under constrained hardware configurations (e.g., 50-100% aperture) through coordinated flight tests with instrumented aircraft, demonstrating the viability of advanced digital signal processing for maintaining detection ranges and clutter rejection on smaller platforms.
Summary Description: Mark Yeary specializes in the engineering and application of fully digital, polarimetric phased array weather radars, primarily through the development of the Horus system at the University of Oklahoma's ARRC. His research focuses on replacing legacy WSR-88D networks with agile, software-defined radar architectures capable of high-temporal-resolution observations of severe weather microphysics. Key methodological contributions include hybrid optimization techniques for multi-beam synthesis, precise mutual coupling calibration using UAS-based far-field measurements, and advanced digital signal processing for interference mitigation and aircraft tracking. His work bridges electromagnetic antenna design with atmospheric science, enabling enhanced detection of tornadoes, hail, and precipitation dynamics through adaptive beamforming and robust polarimetric data collection.
